y[n] = Σ h[k]x[n − k]; output length len(x) + len(h) − 1.
h(t) = (1/τ)e^(−t/τ); H(s) = 1/(τs + 1); step response 1 − e^(−t/τ).
A first-order sensor follows a ramp with a constant τ-second lag, error a × τ.

G(s) = Y(s)/U(s) for a system at rest; for τ dy/dt = −y + Ku it is K/(τs + 1), with a pole at −1/τ and DC gain K.
A pole at s = −p contributes e^(−pt) with time constant 1/p; the slowest stable pole dominates late behaviour; a pole with positive real part gives growth.
Write G(s)/s as a sum A/s + B/(s + p₁) + …; each coefficient is found by covering its factor and evaluating the rest at its pole.
y(∞) = lim s→0 of sY(s) only if all poles of sY(s) are in the left half-plane; a zero in the right half-plane makes the response start in the wrong direction.
G(s) = ω_n²/(s² + 2ζω_n s + ω_n²) with poles −ζω_n ± jω_d, ω_d = ω_n√(1 − ζ²); ζ = 1 is critical damping and ζ > 1 has no overshoot.
M_p = exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)); t_p = π/ω_d; 2% settling t_s ≈ 4/(ζω_n); ζ for a given M_p is −ln M_p/√(π² + ln² M_p).
|G| = 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) with r = f/f_n; at r = 1 it is 1/(2ζ); ζ near 0.64 to 0.7 gives the flattest response.
Ringing at the natural frequency distorts waveforms with harmonics near it; add damping or raise the natural frequency, and test the line to find both.
20 log₁₀|G|; a factor of 2 is +6.02 dB and of 10 is +20 dB; series elements multiply magnitudes and add phases, so decibels and angles add.
|G| = K/√(1 + (ωτ)²), φ = −atan(ωτ); at the corner ω = 1/τ the magnitude is 3.01 dB down and the phase is −45°; above it the magnitude falls 20 dB per decade.
e^(−θs) has magnitude 1 and phase −ωθ rad (−57.30 ωθ degrees): no gain change, phase lag growing with frequency; time lag = phase (rad)/ω.
Drive with small sinusoids at several frequencies; the amplitude ratio gives the magnitude and the time shift gives the phase, −360 × shift/period.
Gain crossover: |L| = 1; phase margin PM = 180° + ∠L there. Phase crossover: ∠L = −180°; gain margin GM = 1/|L| there.
DM = PM (rad)/ω_gc, the extra delay that brings the loop to the edge of instability; the largest stable gain is the present gain times GM.
Typical targets: PM at least 45° and GM at least 2 (6 dB). For second-order-like loops ζ ≈ PM/100 in degrees; a low margin means a ringing closed loop.
A higher gain moves the gain crossover up, where the lag and the delay cost more phase, so the phase margin falls.
C(s) = K_p(1 + 1/(T_i s)), K_i = K_p/T_i; the integral must be constant in steady state, so the error is zero for a step setpoint in a stable loop.
T_i = τ and K_p = τ/(K(λ + θ)) give L = (K_pK/τ)e^(−θs)/s: ω_gc = K_pK/τ and PM = 90° − ω_gc θ; a larger λ means a slower loop and more margin.
From K_u and P_u: PI K_p = 0.45 K_u, T_i = P_u/1.2; PID 0.6 K_u, P_u/2, P_u/8. Aggressive; check the margin.
Integral accumulates while the actuator saturates (K_i × error × time) and overshoots later; clamp the integral or use back-calculation. Filter derivative action.
Sampling at f_s represents only f < f_s/2; a component above that appears at |f − n f_s|, and filtering after sampling cannot remove it.
A low-pass filter before the converter; a first-order RC has amplitude ratio 1/√(1 + (f/f_c)²), which is gentle, so use higher order or oversampling.
A zero-order hold lags by T/2, costing ω T/2 of phase; sample at least ten times per closed-loop time constant.
u[k] = u[k−1] + K_p(e[k] − e[k−1]) + K_p(T/T_i)e[k]; a first-order lag becomes y[k+1] = a y[k] + K(1 − a)u[k] with a = e^(−T/τ). Clamp the stored output.
Count runs and samples separately; the settled value is the mean of the last few samples over the runs; the gain is the settled rise divided by the step.
Delay: the last time the response is still within 2% of its settled value; t63 is the time to reach 63.2%; for a first-order plant with delay, τ = t63 − θ.
Compare the gains from different step sizes; a falling gain means the plant is only approximately linear and the loop gain varies over the range.
They give a model, not a margin: saturation, disturbances and sensor filters need closed-loop tests and measured stability margins.

cards.front: Why the filter makes the loop ring
cards.back: A filter adds phase lag −atan(ωτ_f) at the crossover and lowers the gain, so the phase margin falls; the loop is not changed in gain but the margin is.
A slower filter removes more noise but costs more phase; options are a lower gain, a faster filter, lead (which amplifies noise) or filtering the logged signal outside the loop.
Set the phase at the crossover to −180° + PM, solve for ω_gc and take the gain that makes |L| = 1 there; for the cancelled PI loop K_p = (τ/K) ω√(1 + (ωτ_f)²).
Baseline step; predict the margin; change one thing at a time; measure the margins; test saturation with anti-windup and a disturbance; check robustness; log the settings.
